articles.title: Patrus Ananias defende pagamento do piso nacional do magistério | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato do PT ao governo de Minas cumpriu agenda em Juiz de Fora nesta quarta-feira (30) e apresentou propostas para a educação.
articles.summary: Candidato do PT ao governo de Minas cumpriu agenda em Juiz de Fora nesta quarta-feira (30) e apresentou propostas para a educação.
articles.body:
O candidato do PT ao governo de Minas Gerais, Patrus Ananias, cumpriu agenda de campanha, nesta quarta-feira (30), em Juiz de Fora, na Zona da Mata.

No início da tarde, o candidato atendeu a imprensa em um hotel na região central da cidade. Durante o compromisso, reforçou prioridades do plano de governo e destacou propostas voltadas para a educação.

Patrus Ananias afirmou que, caso seja eleito, pretende oferecer educação pública de qualidade, fortalecer o ensino em tempo integral e garantir o pagamento do piso nacional dos professores em Minas Gerais.

"Educação de qualidade. Com a melhoria do salário das professoras, professores, estabelecendo o piso nacional em Minas Gerais, que não é pago. Professoras e professores do nosso estado recebem abaixo do piso salarial. Nós vamos também batalharmos muito para estabelecer uma escola a tempo integral."

Em seguida, Patrus Ananias participou de um evento com o presidente Lula (PT), candidato à reeleição à Presidência da República, na região central de Juiz de Fora. Também estiveram presentes as candidatas ao Senado Marília Campos (PT) e Áurea Carolina (PSOL).

A forte chuva que atingiu a cidade durante a tarde provocou o cancelamento de uma caminhada que estava prevista na agenda. No lugar, os candidatos foram a um ato político na Praça da Estação, acompanhado por apoiadores e eleitores.

articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro pede ao STF que Dino seja afastado de casos envolvendo ele, Lula e eleições | G1
articles.standfirst: Defesa de Flávio pede ao presidente da Corte que Dino seja afastado de ações envolvendo o senador e Lula e quer suspensão e redistribuição de processos relatados pelo ministro.
articles.summary: Defesa de Flávio pede ao presidente da Corte que Dino seja afastado de ações envolvendo o senador e Lula e quer suspensão e redistribuição de processos relatados pelo ministro.
articles.body:
A defesa do senador e candidato à Presidência Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ) apresentou ao presidente do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ), ministro Edson Fachin, um pedido para que o ministro Flávio Dino seja declarado suspeito para atuar em processos relacionados ao parlamentar, ao presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) e às eleições deste ano.

No pedido, os advogados solicitam, em caráter liminar, a suspensão da tramitação de todas as ações sob relatoria de Dino que tratem de Lula, da disputa presidencial de 2026 ou de Flávio Bolsonaro, até que o STF decida sobre a suspeição do ministro.

A defesa argumenta que o ministro teria uma relação de proximidade com o presidente Lula e pede que os casos sejam redistribuídos a outro integrante da Corte, caso não haja prevenção de outro ministro.

Entre os processos citados pela defesa estão ações sobre o uso de emendas parlamentares, o financiamento do filme Dark Horse e pedidos apresentados pelo PT ao Supremo.

"A suspensão não prejudica investigação. Investigações, se e quando cabíveis, devem prosseguir, com eficiência e profundidade, mas perante o juízo imparcial e competente"diz a defesa no pedido.

"O que não se pode admitir, sempre respeitosamente, é que, a poucos dias da eleição presidencial, continuem sob a relatoria do Exmo. Min. Flávio Dino as causas que envolvem o Presidente, a eleição e o principal adversário do Presidente. Suspender, aqui, não é tomar partido. É obstar o conflito e preservar a imagem da Suprema Corte", complementa.

Segundo os advogados, o objetivo é garantir a imparcialidade dos julgamentos e preservar a "regularidade das eleições de 2026".

Como argumento, a defesa cita a trajetória política de Dino e declarações públicas em apoio a Lula.

Flávio Dino será o segundo a votar no julgamento de Bolsonaro no STF — Foto: Rosinei Coutinho/STF

articles.title: Voto para senador e deputado: maioria está indecisa, diz Datafolha | G1
articles.standfirst: Pesquisa entrevistou 2.016 pessoas com 16 anos ou mais; a margem de erro é de 2 pontos percentuais com nível de confiança de 95%.
articles.summary: Pesquisa Datafolha aponta que a maioria dos eleitores ainda não definiu o voto para senador e deputado às vésperas da votação de domingo.
articles.body:
Cúpula do Senado Federal e prédio do Congresso Nacional durante o amanhecer. — Foto: Pedro França/Agência Senado

A maioria dos brasileiros ainda não decidiu seu voto para senador, deputado federal e deputado estadual, segundo pesquisa Datafolha divulgada nesta quarta-feira (30). O primeiro turno das eleições será no próximo domingo (4).

O percentual de indecisos é maior quando se trata das vagas ao Senado. Segundo o levantamento, 59% dos participantes disseram que ainda não definiram seus votos para senador ou senadora. Outros 14% afirmaram ter escolhido apenas um nome, para uma das duas vagas, enquanto 27% declararam já ter decidido os dois candidatos em quem vão votar.

No caso dos deputados federais, 57% disseram que ainda não definiram o voto, enquanto 43% afirmaram já ter escolhido um candidato.

Quando se trata de deputados estaduais, os percentuais são os mesmos: 57% ainda não se decidiram, contra 43% que já sabem em quem vão votar.

O Datafolha ouviu 2.016 brasileiros com 16 anos ou mais entre os dias 28 e 29 de setembro. A margem de erro é de 2 pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos. O nível de confiança é de 95%.

Entre os que se declararam apoiadores do PT do presidente Lula, 56% disseram não ter definido seu voto para o Senado. Entre apoiadores do PL de Flávio Bolsonaro, o percentual de indefinidos foi de 39%. As margens de erro para PT e PL são de 4 e 6 pontos, respectivamente.

Quando se trata de deputado federal, 54% dos apoiadores do PT disseram não saber ainda em quem vão votar. Já entre os apoiadores do PL, 40% declarou não ter escolhido um candidato.

Já a escolha de deputado estadual tem resultados parecidos. 54% dos que preferem o PT disseram não ter escolhido seu candidato, em comparação com 41% dos apoiadores do PL.

articles.title: Lula cancela agenda em Juiz de Fora por causa do mau tempo | G1
articles.standfirst: Ato político aconteceria no Centro da cidade. Aeronave do presidente chegou a pousar na região, mas helicóptero não tinha condições para voo com segurança até Juiz de Fora.
articles.summary: Ato político aconteceria no Centro da cidade. Aeronave do presidente chegou a pousar na região, mas helicóptero não tinha condições para voo com segurança até Juiz de Fora.
articles.body:
O presidente Lula , candidato à reeleição pelo PT, precisou cancelar a agenda política em Juiz de Fora devido às condições climáticas na cidade, atingida por um temporal na tarde desta quarta-feira (30).

A aeronave do presidente chegou a pousar no Aeroporto Regional da Zona da Mata, em Goianá , a cerca de 40 quilômetros de Juiz de Fora, mas, por conta do mau tempo, não houve teto para o helicóptero que ele usaria até chegar em Juiz de Fora decolar em segurança . Com isso, ele retornaria para Brasília.

Avenida dos Andradas, em Juiz de Fora, ficou alagada após temporal — Foto: Reprodução

Lula cumpriria agenda na cidade da Zona da Mata mineira acompanhado do candidato ao governo de Minas Patrus Ananias e das concorrentes ao Senado, Marília Campos (PT) e Áurea Carolina (PSOL).

O ato político foi mantido com os demais candidatos na Praça da Estação, tradicional ponto de encontro do Partido dos Trabalhadores na cidade.

Lula cumpriria agenda em Juiz de Fora — Foto: REUTERS/Ricardo Moraes

As regiões da Zona da Mata e do Campo das Vertentes estão em alerta para tempestades nas próximas horas e dias. Segundo o Inmet, há previsão de chuva forte, ventos intensos e possibilidade de queda de granizo entre até sexta-feira (2).

O alerta abrange Juiz de Fora, Viçosa , Ubá , Muriaé , São João del Rei e Barbacena .

articles.title: Aliado de Alcolumbre, Rodrigo Pacheco toma posse como ministro do TCU  | G1
articles.standfirst: Ex-presidente do Senado assume cadeira que era ocupada pelo ex-ministro Bruno Dantas. Aos 49 anos, Pacheco poderá ficar no TCU até os 75 anos de idade.
articles.summary: Ex-presidente do Senado assume cadeira que era ocupada pelo ex-ministro Bruno Dantas. Aos 49 anos, Pacheco poderá ficar no TCU até os 75 anos de idade.
articles.body:
Rodrigo Pacheco, novo ministro do TCU — Foto: Edilson Rodrigues/Agência Senado

O ex-presidente do Senado Rodrigo Pacheco tomou posse nesta quarta-feira (30) como ministro do Tribunal de Contas da União (TCU), mas não participou daquela que seria sua primeira sessão plenária após assumir o cargo.

No início dos trabalhos, o presidente da Corte, ministro Vital do Rêgo, informou que Pacheco apresentou uma justificativa para a ausência.

Ele passa a ocupar a vaga aberta com a saída de Bruno Dantas, que renunciou ao cargo para atuar na iniciativa privada.

De perfil discreto, o novo ministro dispensou cerimônia pública de boas-vindas. A posse ocorreu em um ato reservado realizado pela manhã na sede da Corte de Contas, em Brasília, com a presença de autoridades dos três Poderes.

Participaram da cerimônia o vice-presidente da República, Geraldo Alckmin; os ministros do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) Gilmar Mendes, Alexandre de Moraes, Kassio Nunes Marques e Cristiano Zanin; além do procurador-geral da República, Paulo Gonet.

Na semana passada, os ministros do TCU atestaram que Pacheco cumpria os requisitos constitucionais para assumir o cargo. Natural de Porto Velho (RO) e criado em Minas Gerais, ele é advogado formado pela Pontifícia Universidade Católica de Minas Gerais (PUC Minas), com atuação na área de direito penal.

Pacheco iniciou a carreira política como deputado federal por Minas Gerais, em 2014. Na Câmara dos Deputados, presidiu a Comissão de Constituição e Justiça (CCJ) antes de ser eleito senador, em 2018.

Em fevereiro de 2021, foi eleito presidente do Senado com amplo apoio partidário e acabou reconduzido ao comando da Casa para o mandato seguinte. Durante sua gestão, destacou-se pela interlocução entre os Poderes e pela defesa da estabilidade institucional e dos ritos democráticos.

Durante a atuação no Congresso Nacional, Pacheco participou da articulação de propostas como a chamada PEC da Transição e apresentou projetos relacionados à regulamentação da inteligência artificial e à atualização do Código Civil.

E, ao longo da trajetória política, passou por MDB e DEM, migrou para o PSD e, mais recentemente, filiou-se ao PSB.

A indicação de Rodrigo Pacheco para o TCU foi aprovada pelo Senado em 1º de setembro, poucos dias após o anúncio da renúncia de Dantas, em votação realizada diretamente no plenário, sem análise prévia da Comissão de Assuntos Econômicos (CAE).

No dia seguinte, a Câmara dos Deputados confirmou a indicação por 404 votos favoráveis e 61 contrários. Após a aprovação nas duas Casas, o ato foi promulgado pelo Congresso Nacional.

O nome de Pacheco foi articulado pelo presidente do Senado, Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), após a abertura da vaga decorrente da saída antecipada de Bruno Dantas.

O TCU tem, entre as atribuições, apreciar contas prestadas anualmente pelo presidente da República e fiscalizar a aplicação de recursos da União.

O tribunal é composto por nove ministros titulares, dos quais:

seis indicados pelo Congresso (três pela Câmara e três pelo Senado);

três indicados pelo presidente da República (um de forma direta e outros dois entre os ministros-substitutos e membros do Ministério Público junto ao TCU).

A Constituição estabelece que, para ocupar a vaga de ministro do TCU, é necessário ter mais de 35 anos e menos de 65 anos, idoneidade moral e reputação ilibada e também notórios conhecimentos jurídicos, contábeis, econômicos, financeiros ou de administração pública.

O cargo é vitalício, com aposentadoria compulsória aos 75 anos.

articles.title: Leonardo Avalanche renuncia à candidatura à Presidência pelo PRTB | G1
articles.standfirst: Em comunicado, presidente do PRTB criticou "quem apoia um cidadão da pseudodireita'; declaração ocorre um dia após Pablo Marçal (PRTB) anunciar apoio a Flávio Bolsonaro (PL). Avalanche era candidato a vice na chapa de Marçal, que foi considerada inapta pelo TSE
articles.summary: Leonardo Avalanche renuncia à candidatura à Presidência pelo PRTB e critica a 'pseudodireita' após aliança entre Pablo Marçal e Flávio Bolsonaro.
articles.body:
O influenciador Pablo Marçal e o presidente do PRTB, Leonardo Avalanche — Foto: Reprodução/Instagram

O presidente do PRTB, Leonardo Avalanche , anunciou nesta quarta-feira (30) a renúncia à candidatura à Presidência da República. Em comunicado para imprensa, ele afirmou que deixa a disputa por “motivos técnicos, jurídicos e pessoais” e disse que não apoiará nenhum dos candidatos que permanecem na corrida eleitoral.

Avalanche assumiu a candidatura do PRTB depois de o Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) indeferir o registro da chapa de Pablo Marçal. A decisão levou o partido a substituir Marçal por seu presidente na disputa.

No comunicado desta quarta, Avalanche criticou o que chamou de “pseudodireita” e afirmou ficar “impressionado” ao ver “pessoas de bem” apoiarem um “cidadão da pseudodireita”.

“Fico impressionado em ver pessoas de bem apoiarem um cidadão da pseudodireita envolvido em tantos escândalos — entre eles, rachadinha, corrupção e Banco Master.”

Avalanche não cita nominalmente nenhum candidato no trecho. A declaração foi divulgada um dia depois de Pablo Marçal anunciar apoio ao candidato do PL à Presidência , Flávio Bolsonaro.

Na terça-feira (29), Marçal afirmou que passaria a colaborar com a campanha nas áreas de empreendedorismo e mobilidade social. Flávio disse que os dois tiveram uma “conversa longa” e que Marçal “vem para somar” nessas áreas.

Marçal chegou a ser candidato do PRTB à Presidência. O TSE indeferiu o registro da chapa formada por ele e Avalanche em 14 de setembro. Depois da decisão, Avalanche deixou a posição de vice e passou a encabeçar a chapa do partido.

articles.title: Cury diz que Flávio Bolsonaro ‘não é tanto de direita’ e critica Lula | G1
articles.standfirst: Em entrevista ao podcast Inteligência Ltda., candidato também citou um possível convite a Leandro Daiello para comandar a Polícia Federal e acusou Lula de usar o Bolsa Família para obter votos.
articles.summary: No podcast Inteligência Ltda., Cury situou Flávio entre centro e esquerda, citou Daiello para a PF e acusou Lula de usar o Bolsa Família para obter votos.
articles.body:
O candidato à Presidência Augusto Cury (Avante) afirmou nesta quarta-feira (30), em entrevista ao podcast Inteligência Ltda., que Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) “não é tanto de direita” e o situou politicamente entre o centro e a esquerda.

“Eu quero dizer para você que Flávio não é tanto de direita, não, viu?”, declarou. Após o apresentador comentar que há quem coloque Flávio no centro, Cury respondeu: “Centro até para a esquerda”.

Ao defender uma gestão com empreendedorismo, liberdade de negócios e Estado enxuto, Cury também criticou o adversário por, segundo ele, não aceitar o contraditório.

Augusto Cury em entrevista a podcast — Foto: Divulgação

Cury citou a possibilidade de chamar Leandro Daiello, que foi diretor-geral da Polícia Federal entre 2011 e 2017, nos governos Dilma Rousseff e Michel Temer, para comandar a corporação ou o Ministério da Segurança em um eventual governo.

“Pode voltar ao governo, talvez dirigindo a Polícia Federal ou até mesmo o Ministério da Segurança”, afirmou.

O candidato também defendeu a construção de pelo menos mais dois presídios federais e uma força-tarefa que reúna diferentes forças de segurança.

Na mesma entrevista, Cury chamou o “pacote de bondades” do governo Lula de “maldade” e acusou o presidente de usar o aumento do Bolsa Família para obter votos.

“E vamos falar agora do pacote de bondades. Na verdade, maldade do Lula, porque o Lula, número um, ele colocou 15% a mais no Bolsa Família a 17 dias da eleição. Número um, indica que ele não ama os pobres, porque alguém que ama os pobres deveria ter feito isso no começo do ano. E por que não 30%? É porque é usar a dor das pessoas para ter votos", afirmou.

🔎 Lula anunciou em 17 de setembro, a 17 dias do primeiro turno, um reajuste de cerca de 15% nos benefícios do Bolsa Família, elevando o piso de R$ 600 para R$ 691 . Os pagamentos com os novos valores começam em 19 de outubro, antes do segundo turno. Segundo o governo, a medida recompõe a inflação acumulada desde março de 2023 e será custeada dentro das regras fiscais, com remanejamento de recursos do Orçamento.

Durante a entrevista, o candidato afirmou que tentará uma conversa com o presidente do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), ministro Edson Fachin, para tratar da crise na Corte. Segundo Cury, é preciso acabar com a "espetacularização" dos julgamentos e divulgar os resultados apenas para as partes envolvidas com cada análise.

"STF tem que ser discreto, eles são empregados da sociedade, devia ter o máximo de descrição. Eu vou chamar, conversar com o doutor Fachin e com membros do STF porque eu sei que ele é um leitor carinhoso dos meus livros. Tem que terminar com essa espetacularidade da transmissão ao vivo, tem que gravar e distribuir para as partes", afirmou.

De acordo com Cury, caso eleito, ele levará ao Congresso Nacional a proposta de mandato de 8 anos para ministros do Supremo. "Alguém que entra como o doutro Toffoli, com 41 anos, sai com 75?! Ah, pelo amor de Deus! Tem que ser 8 anos para ir embora para nunca mais votar", disse.

articles.title: GOP challenger tears into Dem's 'moderate' image: 'Votes with the squad 90% of the time'
articles.summary: Scott Singer, GOP candidate in FL-25, denounces Democrat incumbent Rep. Jared Moskowitz's voting record, alliance with "the squad," and calls into question his support for Israel.
articles.body: Republican congressional candidate Scott Singer is making the case that party, not just policy, will be decisive in his closely watched South Florida showdown with Democrat Rep. Jared Moskowitz, arguing that the incumbent’s moderate, pro-Israel image is at odds with his voting record and the direction of the Democrat Party. Singer, the former mayor of Boca Raton, told Fox News Digital that he believes his record of cutting taxes and reducing crime at the local level, combined with unwavering support for Israel, gives voters a clear contrast in Florida’s newly redrawn 25th Congressional District. "Well, it is a tough cycle, but people understand the real Jared Moskowitz, one who votes with the squad 90% of the time, voted to put [Rep.] Ilhan Omar [D-Minn.] on the Foreign Affairs Committee, has passed no bills in Congress, but traded $4.5 million worth of stocks since he's been there. This district, after redistricting, is now a Republican plus five district," Singer told Fox News Digital. GOP'S SINGER 'VERY PREPARED' TO OUST DEM MOSKOWITZ IN TOSS-UP FLORIDA RACE THAT COULD DETERMINE HOUSE MAJORITY "It takes in all of Boca Raton, where I was mayor for eight years, cut taxes, red tape, and crime, and goes down to Miami Beach, where I was born, and Fort Lauderdale, where I was raised," he continued. "Moskowitz doesn't live in the district, he's not from the district. "But beyond that, the Republican plus five, a trend in Jewish voters, of which we have 25% … in our district, moving more conservatively, and people who are opposed to socialism and communism, which he will not denounce, understand that this is a critical race for House leadership, and they want someone like me, a local leader with a record of results." Singer's business-friendly fiscal conservatism is the cornerstone of his campaign, and provides the policy framework for his priorities on Capitol Hill. "Well, it gives me the record of results one would need. As mayor of Boca Raton, not only did we have the lowest property tax rate of any full-service city in Florida, I cut the tax rate seven times. I cut red tape, 21 streamlining initiatives," he said. "I cut crime by more than 25% from what were 40-year lows. Those are a record of results that people can relate to, because we improved the quality of life, improved the job base, lowered taxes, and made our streets safer." UNEARTHED AUDIT EXPOSES VULNERABLE DEM'S HANDLING OF COVID RELIEF FUNDS: 'GROSS OVERSIGHT' Singer continued: "That's what we want right now in America. We want secure borders, not like the porous borders that Jared Moskowitz supported under [former] President [Joe] Biden that have increased crime and ravaged communities. They want tax relief, not the tax hike that he voted for. $4 trillion, including taxes on Social Security, tipped workers, small businesses and families that are hurting. Now he's trying to come around with a modest talk of the gas tax reduction. "He had the chance to vote on taxes and repeatedly has voted for higher taxes. People want a leader with a record of results. That's what I bring." While Moskowitz has carefully cultivated a moderate image during his tenure in Congress, Singer disputes that characterization. "No, he's not. He's been voting in lockstep. He's already said he'll vote for whoever the Democratic leadership is. And you can see that we'll have committee chairs like [Rep.] Rashida Tlaib [D-Mich.] and AOC [Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y.], if heaven forbid, the Democrats win Congress," Singer said. "He already voted for Ilhan Omar on Foreign Affairs, despite his talking about her statements being bad, he voted to keep her in charge of foreign affairs in our country." FLORIDA GOP NOMINEE BLASTS 20-YEAR DEM INCUMBENT AS A ‘SOCIALIST’ RUBBER-STAMP WITH ‘PRECIOUS LITTLE TO SHOW’ Added Singer: "He's voted for tax hikes again … He says he's strong on Israel, but he voted against US-Israeli cooperation, when other Democrats were willing to cross the aisle. And then just a few weeks ago, he would not denounce socialism, even though other Democrats would. He's trying to have it out both ways, but his record is really Democratic, really liberal, 90% with the squad." Both Moskowitz and Singer both position themselves as strong supporters of Israel, but Singer argues that membership in today's Democrat Party makes effective advocacy for Israel difficult. "I'm a stronger supporter for Israel. I would never have put Ilhan Omar on the Foreign Affairs Committee. I would not have, like he did, voted against U.S.-Israel cooperation in the NDAA [National Defense Authorization Act]," Singer said. "I would have not voted to undercut President [Donald] Trump's efforts and our military's efforts with the War Powers Act vote months ago when the U.S. and Israel were fighting against a common enemy. "He's done all of those things because Democratic leadership requires him. And he admitted three weeks ago to Jewish Insider that he's being ostracized in his own party. He doesn't have any more chits to give in. He has to go with the way the majority is going, and that expanded squad is going to tamp out any voice he has. "In my party, support for Israel is a feature, not a bug, and I don't have to moderate my views or vote in accordance with the majority…I can be a strong supporter for Israel without reservation. Jared's admitted he can't be and won't be." Finally, while Singer said he is a strong supporter of the Trump administration's military engagement in Iran, he would like to see an end to the conflict soon. "I think we need to have a resolution of this. I think we need to emerge victoriously. We have to remember that nuclear Iran is an existential threat," he said. "We have seen how dastardly, vicious, murderous this regime has been over 47 years. Their foreign policy is death to America. They've killed Americans, they'll kill more. articles.title: Unearthed clip exposes the Talarico comment that triggered backlash from parents
articles.summary: James Talarico, the Democratic Texas U.S. Senate candidate, dismissed parents' concerns about pornography in schools as a "conspiracy theory" at a 2022 hearing.
articles.body: James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas, once dismissed public outcry about explicit material in Texas public schools as a kind of "conspiracy theory" at a July 2022 hearing on education. "We’re going to spend hours hearing bills that are just kind of conspiracy theory-driven and kind of kooky stuff. And we’re going to hear some of that today, I think, in the public testimony — not the invited testimony, but the public testimony," Talarico said then as a member of the Texas House of Representatives. The resurfaced moment adds to the pile of past statements dealing with gender, immigration and law enforcement, complicating the political calculus for Talarico as he aims to convince voters in Texas that, even as a Democrat, he could represent a Republican-leaning constituency in the Lone Star State. TED CRUZ, CONSERVATIVES RESPOND AFTER TALARICO CRITICIZES BIBLE-RELATED EDUCATION IN SCHOOLS AS 'PROPAGANDA' At the time of the 2022 hearing, many parents were raising concerns about news that schools and libraries across the country were featuring explicit materials that bordered on pornography. In particular, an Ashland, Ohio, board meeting made news after a group of angry parents highlighted graphic illustrations from books like "It’s Perfectly Normal," "Making a Baby," "Own Your Period" and "Puberty is Gross but Also Really Awesome," all titles featuring some level of sexual references. Similar outcries emerged in Kentucky, Oregon and North Carolina. In Texas, state Rep. Matt Krause, a Republican, sparked similar backlash when he circulated a list of roughly 800 titles he believed were inappropriate for students. He expressed his alarm in a letter to Texas school districts. "I am writing to you as the Chairman of the Texas House Committee on General Investigation," Krause wrote. "The committee may initiate inquiries concerning any ‘matter the committee considers necessary for the information of the legislature or for the welfare and protection of state citizens.’ "Please identify any other books or content in your district, specifying the campus location and funds spent on acquisition that address or contain … sexually explicit images, graphic presentations of sexual behavior that is in violation of the law or contain material that might make students feel discomfort, guilt, anguish or any other form of psychological distress because of their race or sex or convey that a student, by virtue of their race or sex is inherently racist sexist or oppressive whether consciously or unconsciously." CONTROVERSIAL TEACHER TRAINING TARGETS PARENTAL AUTHORITY AS OPPRESSION, EDUCATION EXPERT WARNS In January 2022, several counties began evaluating their own books, leading some, like Granbury Independent School District, to pull 130 titles from shelves. By July, the issue had made its way before the Texas Legislature in the form of an "interim charge," made by Republican Texas House Speaker Dade Phelan. It was a kind of exhortation for lawmakers to examine the issue, charging them to "monitor and analyze the state policy on curriculum and instructional materials used in public schools." As a part of the Committee on Public Education, Talarico received the charge but expressed reservations about its substance, making his "conspiracy theory" comment. He went on to ask Texas Education Agency Commissioner Mike Morath about the issue. "I want to ask you about curriculum in Texas, of course, critical race theory, pornography; these are the things we see bubbling up on social media that’s going to be discussed here," Talarico said. "Are you aware of any curriculum in the state of Texas that, one, bullies students based on their race or, two, grooms students with pornography?" Morath, after noting that Texas is a very big state and the issue is "very complex," gave his blunt assessment. "The answer is yes," Morath said. "We have complaints that would appear to substantiate periodic problems in those areas, arguably. I can’t tell you it’s widespread. We’ve reviewed, in some cases, materials that were made available to students that I think the common citizen would agree would be inappropriate." CARVILLE ADVISES TALARICO 'TO DEAL WITH' PAST CULTURE WAR COMMENTS IF HE WANTS TO WIN TEXAS Even after the testimony, Talarico challenged the idea that explicit materials in schools were widespread. "I would characterize as a conspiracy theory that’s being raised is that these are systemic policy problems in the state of Texas," Talarico said. Following Talarico’s remarks, parents spoke out against his characterization. "I actually drove in last night, so I’ve been here a very long time. And hopefully my comments and testimony today aren’t gonna be as ‘kooky’ as Representative Talarico had stated it was gonna be," one parent quipped. articles.title: Trump Pentagon launches competition for America's next great military base
articles.summary: The winning state for the base site will be selected through a merit-based competition based on land, housing, schools, community support and regulatory cooperation.
articles.body: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth on Wednesday announced plans to build a modern, self-sustaining military fortress, saying the site will be selected through a merit-based competition among governors pitching their states as potential locations. The megaproject, dubbed the "Next Great American Base," was unveiled during an address at Marine Corps Base Quantico as part of Hegseth’s six strategies to modernize the military. The initiative rejects what Hegseth described as the legacy approach to spend heavily on advanced weapons systems while service members live on aging bases with outdated barracks. "For too long, our military has been bogged down by the same old tired Washington playbook: spending trillions on exquisite weapons systems, while our troops live in aging bases, outdated barracks, and with inadequate infrastructure. That era is over," Hegseth said. EXCLUSIVE: HEGSETH TO DOUBLE CUTS TO GENERALS, ADMIRALS IN MAJOR PENTAGON SHAKEUP "To back up our warfighters, when we bring the troops home, we won’t just reshuffle troops onto legacy posts. We are going to build them beautiful new bases from the ground up," he added. The ambitious undertaking will feature a brand-new military installation spanning hundreds of thousands of acres and housing up to 25,000 service members. "We are talking hundreds of thousands of acres with organic power generation, modern air defenses, and cutting edge technology — a fortress," he said. The installation is expected to provide first-class living conditions, high-end training grounds and essential services such as health care and child care, while operating entirely off the commercial grid with independent power sources. Hegseth added that the base will support President Donald Trump’s executive order on "Beautiful Civic Architecture," which calls for federal public buildings and military installations to be designed in timeless and classical styles. "We owe our warriors nothing less than the gold standard," Hegseth said. SENATE REPUBLICAN PUSHES MERIT-BASED MILITARY PROMOTIONS, TARGETS BIDEN-ERA DEI POLICIES To determine the site location, the Department of War said it is launching a transparent, merit-based competition in which state governors can pitch their proposals directly to top military leadership at the Pentagon. The winning state will be chosen based on its ability to remove regulatory hurdles and bureaucracy to speed up construction, while offering the best package of land, community support, top-tier housing, schools and other services. "The state that cuts the most red tape and offers the best package of land and support will win the historic honor of hosting the most lethal, modern, and beautiful military installation on the planet," a press release stated. Pitch deliberations will be recorded and made public to eliminate "political favoritism," according to the Pentagon. "No backroom Washington deals. No political favoritism – just a straight-up, merit-based contest to see which state will partner with us to build the most modern, beautiful, and lethal military installation on the planet," Hegseth said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The project is the fourth announcement among six major strategic initiatives unveiled by the secretary. According to the Department of War, the other initiatives focus on restoring male physical standards and combat roles, improving the comprehensive review of military standards, overhauling complaint processes, reforming senior leadership and focusing on core training and maintenance.

articles.title: Elon Musk lands new Trump administration role shaping future of American warfare
articles.summary: Elon Musk will co-lead Project Meridian with Palmer Luckey and Newt Gingrich to map future warfare domains and military technologies for the Pentagon.
articles.body: Elon Musk is taking on a new role in the Trump administration, this time helping the Pentagon determine which weapons and technology American troops will need to fight the wars of the future. War Secretary Pete Hegseth announced Wednesday that Musk will co-lead Project Meridian, a new Pentagon initiative tasked with looking years and even decades ahead to identify emerging domains of warfare and the capabilities the U.S. military will need to dominate them. Musk, the former leader of the Trump administration's Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), will lead the effort alongside defense tech billionaire Palmer Luckey and former House Speaker Newt Gingrich under the direction of War Department Chief Technology Officer Emil Michael. EXCLUSIVE: HEGSETH TO DOUBLE CUTS TO GENERALS, ADMIRALS IN MAJOR PENTAGON SHAKEUP "The best forecasters of future conflict do not solely reside inside the Pentagon," Hegseth said during his State of the Force address at Marine Corps Base Quantico. "There are obvious biases and risks to asking ourselves to both ask the questions and answer them." Hegseth said the initiative would begin immediately, and he would meet with Musk, Luckey and Gingrich in a secure site just 200 yards from the stage after his speech. Project Meridian will have 120 days to "ruthlessly map the trajectory of wars, domains and technologies," culminating in a public rollout of its findings and a classified annex. Hegseth described a sweeping mandate that stretches "from under the Earth to beyond the moon." Rather than developing new military strategies or policies, the group will seek to identify "the domains that we must conquer and capabilities we must master" and focus on "discovering, developing and fielding" weapons and systems that could be needed by future generations of American troops. Musk and Luckey enter the effort with firsthand experience developing technology for the U.S. military. Musk's SpaceX is a major Pentagon contractor, while Luckey founded Anduril Industries, a defense technology company specializing in autonomous weapons and other advanced military systems. Their industry experience positions both men to bring an unusually close view of emerging technology and the modern battlefield to the Pentagon's long-range planning. It could also raise potential conflict-of-interest questions as executives whose companies compete for defense business help identify the capabilities and technologies the military should pursue. BATTLEFIELD ROBOTS OPEN NEW FRONT IN INNOVATION WAR WITH MAJOR US ADVERSARY Meridian was one piece of a broader push announced by Hegseth Wednesday to remake the military around autonomous warfare and rapidly emerging technology. Hegseth announced the creation of Autonomous Warfare Command, or AUTOWARCOM, a new four-star combatant command with what he described as "service-like authorities" to scale autonomous and robotic capabilities across the joint force. The War Department will also begin phasing in new occupational frameworks across the military departments to create dedicated career paths for what Hegseth called a new generation of "autonomous warfighters." "We should have been thinking about Autonomous Warfare Command ten years ago," Hegseth said, explaining that Meridian is intended to look far enough ahead to anticipate the next technological transformation before the military falls behind. The announcements came during the second iteration of what the War Department has dubbed Hegseth’s annual State of the Force address at Marine Corps Base Quantico. The setting was the same as last year, but the audience was markedly different. Hegseth summoned generals, admirals and other senior military leaders from around the world to Quantico for his first address, where he laid out sweeping changes to military standards, personnel and what he called the "warrior ethos." This time, Hegseth addressed a younger generation of military leaders, including top-performing E-6 enlisted service members and O-3 officers from across the force. He called them the military’s "current and future leaders on the front lines" and said the address would become an annual opportunity to assess the state of the force and lay out his vision for its future. Hegseth used Wednesday’s speech to unveil six new initiatives, ranging from the military’s embrace of autonomous warfare to an effort to make U.S. bases and defense supply chains less vulnerable to foreign disruption. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The secretary also used the address to deliver some of his most pointed rhetoric yet about his effort to reshape the culture of the military and about the news media. "We are no longer the woke department or the weak department," Hegseth said. "No fatties, no trainees, no weirdos, no beardos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors." Hegseth later accused some journalists of engaging in "partisan activism" that jeopardizes military operations and service members, calling such reporting "fundamentally anti-American." "It’s sick. It’s a national betrayal. It’s treason, actually," Hegseth said.

articles.title: FCC head says government-funded Trump ads are ‘normal’ and ‘don’t raise any red flags’
articles.summary: Brendan Carr said the ads are “normal-course public service announcements” and nothing that would “merit any sort of” review by the Federal Communications Commission.
articles.body: Federal Communications Commission Chair Brendan Carr said Wednesday that new pro-Trump TV ads paid for with government funds don’t “merit any sort of FCC review.” “It doesn’t strike me as anything at all out of the ordinary,” Carr said of the ads, which have aired across the country in recent weeks. Asked about allegations that the ads are “propaganda,” Carr laughed. The White House has “explained that these are just normal-course public service announcements, PSAs, that you see all the time. I don’t think there’s anything unique or different about it,” he said at a news conference. “There’s nothing in there that strikes me that merit any sort of FCC review,” said Carr, whom Trump appointed to the agency. A reporter pointed out that the progressive advocacy group Public Citizen filed a complaint with the FCC noting that the Trump campaign used one of the ads in 2024. Carr brushed off the concern, telling reporters that “there’s groups on the left that have, you know, long worked and pushed to weaponize the FCC’s license renewal process” but that the ads “don’t raise any red flags.” Public Citizen did not immediately respond to a request for comment Wednesday. Anna Gomez, the lone Democratic commissioner on the FCC, told NBC News in a statement, “I recognize the concern shared by others that taxpayer dollars are being used to promote a political message, particularly given the timing of these ads coming so close to an election.” “While it is not surprising to see the FCC exercise a double standard when it comes to its investigative decisions, I am certain we will hear more about this from folks in Congress, who are ultimately responsible,” her statement said. The use of federal funds to pay for the ads has drawn bipartisan criticism, with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., saying they “shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars” and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., calling them an “absolute violation of what democracy is supposed to look like.” Trump defended the ads when asked about them Wednesday in the Oval Office. “I’m not running for office and I don’t talk about anybody,” he said. “When I’m talking about making America great, making our country great, that’s a countrywide ad. That’s an ad for the spirit of our country.” “Now, if somebody said that that’s wrong, I’ll gladly pay the money. But these are ads for the country,” he added. The first of the ads features Trump describing how he wants to “defeat communism” while the song “Love Me” by JMSN plays in the background. Another spot is a slightly shorter version of a 2024 Trump campaign ad, which shows him walking down a hallway as he asks people in a voice-over to join him in his “final battle” to “demolish the deep state” and “expel the warmongers from our government.” In its complaint Tuesday, Public Citizen said that the messages are thinly veiled campaign ads timed to motivate Trump’s supporters ahead of the upcoming midterm elections and that they are unlawful. “Federal law explicitly prohibits using appropriated public funds for government propaganda, self-aggrandizement, or partisan political advertising. Yet, that is exactly the nature of Trump’s recent campaign ads,” the complaint says, adding that none of the ads to date “meet the standard of a public service announcement.” “They do not refer to any specific governmental program and they do not serve the purpose of informing the public about any specific governmental program,” the complaint says. Carr has made headlines for using his post to go after late-night comedians like Stephen Colbert and Jimmy Kimmel and network programs that he has alleged have liberal biases. The FCC issued an order this year directing Disney’s eight owned-and-operated television stations to file their broadcast license renewals ahead of schedule after the White House and ABC clashed over a joke Kimmel made about first lady Melania Trump. Disney is challenging the review with a suit alleging the FCC is seeking to coerce and retaliate against “a network that refuses to bow to the ⁠administration’s ​demands.” Carr has said the ABC license review stems from the FCC’s probe of Disney’s diversity, equity and inclusion practices — not “speech.”

articles.title: Pentagon data breach exposes Social Security numbers, personal info of 2.76M US military, civilian personnel
articles.summary: A Pentagon personnel data breach exposed employment information belonging to both living and deceased U.S. military and civilian personnel.
articles.body: A Pentagon personnel database breach exposed sensitive personal information belonging to 2.76 million living U.S. military and civilian personnel, and 294,000 deceased individuals, a Pentagon official confirmed to Fox News. Unauthorized users accessed unencrypted files containing Social Security numbers and military or civilian employment information between October 2025 and July 2026. The Defense Manpower Data Center (DMDC) discovered the vulnerability in a file-sharing system on July 16 and notified affected individuals Sept. 18. FBI STRIKES BACK AT HACKING GROUP WITH OVERSEAS ARREST OF ALLEGED LEADER A Pentagon official said a few unauthorized users accessed personally identifiable information through the DMDC system during the roughly nine-month period. Upon discovering the vulnerability, the DMDC immediately remediated it, according to the official. The Pentagon said it has no indication the information was misused. PENTAGON REVEALS SECRET SPACE WEAPONS ARE ALREADY IN ORBIT — BUT WON'T SAY WHAT THEY DO Affected individuals are being notified by postal mail through Identity Theft Guard Solutions, or IDX, a provider contracted by the Department of Defense. IDX will provide credit monitoring and identity restoration support to affected individuals based on the types of personal information impacted in each case, according to the Pentagon. The Pentagon directed individuals with questions about the breach to contact IDX through its website or by calling 1-855-744-4556. The DMDC maintains personnel and workforce information for the Defense Department and provides data and services supporting military personnel, their families and other Defense Department operations. FORMER SECRET SERVICE CYBERCRIME EXPERT WEIGHS IN ON PRIVACY AFTER HACKERS BREACH STOLEN FLOCK CAMERA The breach exposed information belonging to more than 3 million living and deceased individuals overall, though the Pentagon said it has not identified evidence that the accessed information has been misused. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Pentagon did not identify the unauthorized users in its statement or provide additional details about how they gained access to the file-sharing system.

articles.title: A California showdown with national implications: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: In today’s edition, we take a look at where the billionaire tax campaign in California stands and what it signals about the Democratic Party’s direction.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, we take a look at where the billionaire tax campaign in California stands and what it signals about the Democratic Party’s direction. Plus, Andrea Mitchell examines President Donald Trump’s efforts to reassure a skeptical public on AI. — Adam Wollner A California showdown with national implications By Adam Wollner and Adam Edelman California Democrats avoided what would have been a brutal and costly intraparty fight for governor when progressive activist Tom Steyer finished third in the all-party primary this summer, leaving former Health Secretary Xavier Becerra as the clear favorite in a one-on-one November matchup against Republican Steve Hilton. But there’s a battle brewing further down the ballot that could have even broader implications for the party, both in the state and nationally. Voters in California will decide this fall whether to implement a one-time 5% tax on the state’s billionaires. Listed as “Proposition 40,” the ballot measure is shaping up as one of the most expensive campaigns in the country this year, with roughly $100 million already spent or booked on ads through Election Day, according to AdImpact. Tech leaders in Silicon Valley, most notably Google co-founder Sergey Brin, have aggressively lined up against the billionaire tax, which was pushed by SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West. As we’ve reported, the proposal emerged as a major fault line for Democrats in the state’s race for governor and in the not-so-invisible 2028 presidential primary. Becerra and term-limited Gov. Gavin Newsom are against it, while Steyer and Rep. Ro Khanna are for it. Meanwhile, a slew of other prominent California Democrats — including former Vice President Kamala Harris, former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and Sens. Adam Schiff and Alex Padilla — have not taken firm public stances on the ballot measure. A new poll out today underscores why the party is scattered on the issue. According to a NBCUniversal Local/Telemundo Station Group survey, 48% of likely California voters back the billionaire tax, while 38% oppose it and 14% are undecided. While it’s certainly a more promising result for proponents of the measure than opponents, it still falls short of majority support. Among Democrats, however, 67% said they will vote for the proposal and 19% said they will vote against it.One of the arguments from the anti-billionaire-tax side is that wealthy Californians will flee the state. The poll showed that 59% of respondents said they were not concerned about that potential outcome, compared to 41% who said they were concerned. Passage of a first-of-its-kind billionaire tax would be a major shot in the arm for progressives heading into the 2028 campaign. While deep-blue California is not necessarily representative of the entire nation, a victory would further highlight the populist streak running through the party’s base and the electorate at large. A national NBC News poll earlier this month asked registered voters whether 15 different attributes would make them more or less likely to support a candidate. The most popular? Raising taxes on billionaires. That’s the sort of energy potential White House contenders like Khanna are hoping to tap into: He’s set to team up with Sen. Bernie Sanders for rallies in San Francisco and Los Angeles in the coming days in support of the wealth tax. Trump has a new name for AI — but not regulations Analysis by Andrea Mitchell The world’s tech leaders — 21 men and one woman — were out in full force for a White House lunch with President Donald Trump Tuesday. Their cumulative wealth? Hard to estimate. Their promise to voluntarily regulate artificial intelligence? Perhaps equally so. To try to reassure a skittish public about the safety of the biggest technological transformation since the internet, Trump, a master of rebranding, signed an executive order requiring all federal agencies to rename AI as “superintelligence,” or “SI.” With considerable fanfare, the White House heralded a new accord to develop internal safety controls to prevent rogue agents from spinning out of control. The self-policing agreement includes risk reviews and auditing by third parties. Trump called the voluntary agreement “morally binding.” Tech journalist Kara Swisher called it a “pinky promise.” Ironically, the White House position against any regulation came on the same day Anthropic submitted its security filing for its long-awaited IPO. It devoted almost one-third of the filing to warning investors the technology may pose “existential risks to humanity,” including that advanced AI models could manipulate, blackmail and exhibit other unpredictable behaviors. Last April, Anthropic held back its Mythos model citing potential dangers. In July, OpenAI models hacked the Hugging Face AI startup. In September, leaders of Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind called for slowing down advanced models because of safety concerns. And last week, OpenAI revealed its tools had hacked dozens of sites, including governments, and scrapped plans to release its newest model next month. In an interview with “Meet the Press” that aired Sunday, Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates told Kristen Welker, “AI is powerful enough to drive events that cause a billion deaths,” adding, “There’s never been a weapon as powerful as the combination of people with ill intent using the latest AI tools.” Asked about voluntary regulation, he said, “No one thinks self-regulation is enough.” In response to growing political concerns in both parties, Trump said yesterday, “I will never stifle the growth of technology that will be bigger than the industrial revolution.” During a White House summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping, the two rivals in the AI race issued a vague agreement to communicate about threats. At the White House yesterday, competition over AI was top of mind over cooperation. Trump told the tech CEOs, “You’re going to have a winner, or you’re going to have a loser,” adding, “We’re leading now over China and everyone else, and I want to keep it that way.” That same day, Senate Democrats tried to pass legislation to regulate AI by unanimous consent, but Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, objected. The debate has even caught the attention of the pope. Speaking to reporters yesterday, Pope Leo questioned Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s commitment to safety. Huang, who has called for a hands-off approach on regulation, was among the guests at the state dinner for Xi and yesterday’s White House meeting. “He’s the same one, however, that says there should be no limits placed and no government regulation,” the pope said of Huang. He added, “I do think that the concerns raised by many of the experts, specialists in AI, should be taken seriously.” That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner and Lauren Zola. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

articles.title: Fox News Poll: Michigan voters split between El-Sayed and Rogers
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed holds a slim 1-point edge over Mike Rogers in the Michigan senate race as voter concerns about both candidates keep it tight.
articles.body: Michigan voters have concerns about both candidates in the U.S. Senate race and that leads to a tight contest, according to a new Fox News poll. Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has a slim 1-point edge against Republican Mike Rogers, 50-49%, among Michigan likely voters. The survey, released on Wednesday, is the first Fox News Poll this season among likely voters, so a direct comparison can’t be made to previous polls. Yet among registered voters, the preference is almost identical, 51% El-Sayed vs. 48% Rogers. That’s a reversal since August, when Rogers was ahead by 4 points among registered voters, 51% to El-Sayed’s 47%. FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS QUESTION WHETHER AI’S PROMISE OUTWEIGHS ITS RISKS The analysis below is among likely voters, unless otherwise noted. More of El-Sayed’s backers feel certain of their choice (87%) than Rogers’ (80%). Overall, 15% say they could switch their pick before voting, including 18% of Rogers’ supporters and 12% of El-Sayed’s. FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS Here’s why the race is tight. Roughly equal numbers of Michiganders say they are extremely concerned Rogers is too close to President Donald Trump (39%) as say El-Sayed’s views are too liberal (36%). And their favorable ratings are also close: 47% view El-Sayed positively compared to 44% for Rogers. Among registered voters, positive views of El-Sayed increased by 5 points since August while Rogers’ declined by four points. El-Sayed’s best groups include those who traditionally go Democratic: women, Black voters and those with a college degree. He’s also ahead with voters under age 45 and the small subgroup of union households. The groups giving Rogers some of his strongest support include men, rural voters, White evangelical Christians, married voters and Whites without a college degree. Both candidates receive near-universal backing from their party. Rogers receives 95% among Republicans, while it’s 93% for El-Sayed among Democrats. In addition, Rogers gets 99% of MAGA Republicans and 88% of non-MAGA Republicans, while El-Sayed garners 98% of DSA Democrats and 90% of non-DSA Democrats. The small number of independents narrowly favor El-Sayed. This year’s political landscape favors El-Sayed. The Democrats hold a 5-point advantage when voters are asked which party they want to control the Senate, 52% to 47%. But to capitalize on that, he’ll need to consolidate Democratic support after a contentious primary because 11% of likely voters who backed his primary opponent Haley Stevens say they plan to vote for Rogers. CLICK HERE FOR CROSSTABS AND TOPLINE "The Michigan Senate race is unique in that short-term political forces favoring the Democrats are somewhat offset by concerns about the Democratic candidate," says Republican pollster Daron Shaw, who conducts the Fox News Poll with Democrat Chris Anderson. "The bad news for Rogers is El-Sayed has made progress shoring up Democratic support and has room to grow given voter concerns about the economy." Four in ten Michiganders say they are falling behind financially, and they back El-Sayed by 25 points. But the largest share, nearly half, describe their family as holding steady, and they favor Rogers by 13 points, while the small number who are getting ahead prefer Rogers by 36 points. Still, for 7 in 10 voters, the cost of living will be extremely important to their Senate vote, and they back El-Sayed by 13 points. He also has advantages among the 4 in 10 focused on U.S. policy toward Israel (+8 points) and AI technology (+17 points). Conversely, Rogers is favored by 26 points among the 44% focused on immigration. Half of Michigan voters consider Trump extremely important to their Senate vote, and they favor El-Sayed by 22 points. In 2024, Trump won Michigan by less than two percentage points, while Rogers lost to Democrat Elissa Slotkin by less than half a point. Voter frustration with the administration is a drag on Rogers, as nearly 6 in 10 disapprove of the president’s performance. While 40% approve, not all support Rogers (93%). He remains competitive with support from 19% of Trump disapprovers overall, even as 28% who only "somewhat" disapprove of Trump prefer El-Sayed. In the gubernatorial race to replace term-limited Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, Democrat Jocelyn Benson leads Republican John James 54% to 45% among likely voters. Twelve percent of those backing Rogers in the Senate race cross-party lines to favor Benson. Conducted September 24-28, 2026, under the joint direction of Beacon Research (D) and Shaw & Company Research (R), this Fox News Poll includes interviews with a sample of 1,203 Michigan registered voters randomly selected from a statewide voter file. Respondents spoke with live interviewers on landlines (114) and cellphones (794) or completed the survey online after receiving a text message (295). Results based on the registered voter sample have a margin of sampling error of ±2.5 percentage points and for the subsample of 1,028 likely voters it is ±3 percentage points. Sampling error for results among subgroups is higher. In addition to sampling error, question wording and order can influence results. Sources for developing weight targets include the most recent American Community Survey, Fox News Voter Analysis and voter file data. Weights are generally applied to age, race, education and area variables to ensure the demographics of respondents are representative of the registered voter population. Likely voters are based on a probabilistic statistical model that relies on past vote history, interest in the current election, intention to vote, age, education, race, ethnicity and marital status. Results among subgroups are only shown when the sample size is at least N=100. Fox News’ Victoria Balara contributed to this report.

articles.title: Biden Afghan migrant program hit with 40% vetting failure rate: 'Alarming'
articles.summary: A Homeland Security inspector general report found documentation or vetting errors in 40% of Afghan asylum applications reviewed under Operation Allies Welcome, raising concerns.
articles.body: Federal inspectors identified one or more documentation or vetting errors in 40% of asylum applications they reviewed for Afghan nationals admitted under the Biden administration's Operation Allies Welcome program, concluding the deficiencies increased the risk U. S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) could miss information that may have made some applicants ineligible for asylum. The Sept. 23 Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Office of Inspector General report reviewed a sample of 678 asylum applications filed by Afghan nationals admitted through Operation Allies Welcome, the Biden administration initiative launched after the U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan. Inspectors identified 303 missing aliases, 23 missing security checks and more than 150 additional documentation deficiencies, including two cases involving applicants who may have been inadmissible on terrorism-related grounds. FORMER USCIS OFFICIAL, ACCOMPLICE CHARGED IN ALLEGED $960K CITIZENSHIP BRIBERY SCHEME The findings come as Operation Allies Welcome has faced renewed scrutiny following several high-profile arrests of Afghan nationals admitted under the program. Fox News Digital has previously reported on the arrests of an alleged ISIS-K supporter, an Afghan national charged with making terroristic threats and another Afghan national admitted under Operation Allies Welcome who was later arrested after being convicted of indecent exposure to a minor. In a press release, DHS argued the report demonstrated the Biden administration "dangerously mismanaged" Operation Allies Welcome, saying a lawsuit settlement that required USCIS to adjudicate 90% of asylum applications within 150 days forced the agency to prioritize speed over more thorough reviews. The DHS inspector general report, which noted hundreds of aliases had not been recorded for applicants, underscored the importance of accurate record keeping, pointing out one applicant had 124 known aliases. The report said that "missed FBI name checks" accounted for nearly 60% of the absent security checks that the report identified. The report also flagged two asylum applications involving applicants with potential terrorism-related concerns. In one case, required paperwork documenting the government's review was missing entirely. In another, supervisors began the approval process but never completed the final step, leaving no clear record that the review had been finished. ARMY VET LAWMAKER MARKS ABBEY GATE ANNIVERSARY WITH BLISTERING MESSAGE FOR BIDEN-HARRIS: 'ABJECT FAILURE' Mark Krikorian, executive director of the conservative Center for Immigration Studies, said the inspector general's findings reinforce concerns critics have raised since the chaotic Kabul evacuation in 2021. "The fact that 40% of these applications have errors is alarming," Krikorian told Fox News Digital. "This IG report just underlines how superficial and even frivolous the vetting that we were assured was going on was." Krikorian said many evacuees were first flown to temporary processing hubs, sometimes referred to as "lily pads," in third countries before ultimately being admitted to the United States. While those locations allowed U.S. officials to conduct additional processing, he argued the practical reality was that partner countries were not going to permanently accept the evacuees, leaving the United States effectively committed to resettling them. HOMELAND SECURITY OFFICIAL'S KILLING LEAVES AGENCY 'DEVASTATED' AS VETTING BREAKDOWN EXPOSED "As soon as that cargo bay door closed, we're stuck with those people," Krikorian said, noting how the United States effectively committed itself to resettling evacuees once they boarded evacuation flights during the chaotic Kabul withdrawal. Krikorian argued the inspector general's report likely understated the scope of the problem because inspectors could only identify documentation deficiencies visible in the files they reviewed, not determine whether every applicant had been thoroughly vetted. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The inspector general ultimately made five recommendations aimed at strengthening USCIS' review of Operation Allies Welcome asylum applications, including improving documentation of applicant aliases, ensuring required security checks are properly recorded and enhancing oversight of adjudication files. USCIS agreed with all five recommendations, according to the report.

articles.title: Justice Department files complaint against judges over immigration enforcement surge comments
articles.summary: The complaint alleges seven judges violated judicial ethics by speaking to the press about their experience dealing with a flood of cases last winter in the Twin Cities.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The Department of Justice filed a complaint Wednesday against federal judges in Minnesota over their remarks to the media about the pressure on their courthouse during Trump administration’s immigration enforcement surge. The complaint alleges the seven judges — nominated by Democrats and Republican presidents — violated judicial ethics by speaking to The New York Times about their experience dealing with a flood of cases during last winter’s Operation Metro Surge crackdown that led to thousands of arrests in the Twin Cities. The complaint escalates the department’s battle with the federal judiciary, which has halted administration priorities, dismissed high-profile prosecutions and accused government lawyers in some cases of failing to comply with court orders. The department is demanding that the judges recuse themselves from all criminal or civil cases involving the Department of Homeland Security, Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters, because of what he described as “obvious bias they have shown” in their remarks to the newspaper. “When we have a situation like we have now, where you have a judge, a couple of judges, just not only violating the canons in our view, but also showing bias in what they’re saying, we have no choice but to act to defend not only our prosecutors, but also DHS,” Blanche said. The judge at the center of the story, Patrick Schiltz, accused the government in January of failing to comply with nearly 100 court orders. He said in a ruling that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, a part of DHS, “is not a law unto itself.” Schiltz, who was nominated by Republican President George W. Bush and served as a law clerk for Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia, told the newspaper that what happened in Minnesota’s federal court last winter “created a grave threat to the rule of law.” In a statement Wednesday, a spokesperson for the Minnesota court said legal experts have confirmed that the judges were acting “well within the ethical rules that apply to federal judges” in speaking to the newspaper. Schiltz also said in a statement that his comments did not violate any ethical rules. “Indeed, in February of this year, the Committee on Codes of Conduct issued an advisory opinion to emphasize that federal judges” may speak or write “on core judiciary matters such as advocacy for the rule of law and judicial independence,’” Schiltz said in a statement. “That is exactly what I did.” The complaint was filed with the chief judge of the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, which oversees federal judges in Minnesota. The Republican administration has railed against what it describes as “activist judges” who officials say are intent on thwarting Trump’s agenda. Yet some of the most critical and unfavorable court rulings have come from judges nominated by Trump and other Republican presidents.

articles.title: US Senate rejects bill targeting AI data centre electricity costs
articles.summary: Democrats criticise bill as lacking ‘teeth’ and push for mandatory measures to address soaring electricity bills.
articles.body:
The United States Senate has thwarted a bill that would have required state regulators to consider forcing data centres and other major electricity users to bear the costs of the infrastructure built to serve them.

The measure failed by a vote of 57 to 43 on Wednesday. The proposal needed to pass by at least 60 votes to prevent a filibuster, a procedural hurdle in the Senate that can stymie a bill indefinitely.

Only four Democrats — Maggie Hassan, Amy Klobuchar, Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock — joined Republicans to support the bill, which proponents argue would have eased the burden of rising energy costs on individual households.

The artificial intelligence (AI) boom has led to increasing demand for data centres, which provide computing power for the new technology.

There are as many as 5,400 data centres currently in the US, according to some estimates. Critics argue the facilities require substantial amounts of energy to operate, contributing to higher electricity costs.

The Ratepayer Protection Act, a first-of-its-kind bipartisan bill, was aimed at addressing the economic concerns linked to the expansion of data centres.

It passed the House of Representatives earlier this month in a landslide vote of 417 to three.

But Democrats in the Senate argued the bill does not go far enough to protect consumers from high electricity bills. Rather than requiring states to “consider” a federal utility rate standard, some senators advocated instead for mandatory enforcement to guarantee consumer relief.

Other critics described the bill as a last-ditch Republican effort to secure a legislative victory ahead of the November midterm elections.

Senate Democratic Party leader Chuck Schumer, for instance, dismissed the legislation as “toothless”. He noted that the bill failed to require data centres to cover the costs they incur in upgrades to electricity infrastructure.

“We need real action on data centres, and what do Republicans decide all of a sudden to push forward? A bill that is totally optional,” said Schumer.

He challenged Republicans to prove their commitment to the issue by passing a Democratic alternative that “has teeth”.

Despite widespread pushback, thousands of data centres already span the US, with construction underway for dozens more. While the states of Virginia and Texas lead the nation in operating facilities, California, Ohio and New York follow behind closely as top digital infrastructure hubs.

According to a September poll , 53 percent of Americans are “extremely” or “very” concerned about the impact of data centres on electricity prices or water supplies in the communities where they are built.

articles.title: Mamdani's taxpayer-funded influencer army accused of plotting pressure campaign against NYC CEOs
articles.summary: Senior aides to Mayor Zohran Mamdani reportedly discussed mobilizing a 200-plus influencer network against top CEOs and business leaders in New York City.
articles.body: Senior officials in New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's administration are reportedly plotting a coordinated social media pressure campaign against some of the city's most powerful business leaders, looking to mobilize a 200-plus influencer network run through City Hall. Mamdani's network of social media creators working for him first drew scrutiny earlier this month after the Columbia Journalism Review revealed that City Hall was communicating with more than 200 influencers through an encrypted Signal group called "NYC Creators Announcements." Fox News Digital subsequently reported that members receive daily talking points, videos and other updates from the administration, while also being offered access to events and city officials. MAMDANI’S ‘MASS ENGAGEMENT’ OFFICE DRAWS FIRE OVER PLANS TO BUILD INFLUENCE BEYOND CITY HALL: ‘NYC IS DONE’ Now, two sources briefed on the effort told the New York Post that senior City Hall aides have discussed mobilizing the influencer network against New York business executives, including leaders of the Partnership for New York City, an influential nonprofit representing the city's business leaders and largest employers. Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla and Related Companies CEO Jeff Blau have also been floated as potential targets, according to the Post. The reported strategy centers on "blindsid[ing]" Partnership for New York City President and CEO Steven Fulop, who took over the organization earlier this year, with one source telling the Post that aides viewed the leadership transition as an opportunity to "go at CEOs." "They want to punch Fulop in the face," the source told The Post. Fulop, however, told Fox News he personally spoke with Mamdani after the report and that the mayor, his communications director and political director all denied plans to target business executives. Fulop said the Partnership would take Mamdani "at his word" while remaining "vigilant and watchful" but noted if he continued down this path there could be "huge repercussions in a bad way." Mamdani spokesperson Dora Pekec, meanwhile, called the Post's report "categorically false" and "a complete lie," though the Post reported that she declined to identify specific inaccuracies in its account. The Mamdani administration's use of influencers and Signal had already drawn scrutiny before the latest report this week from the New York Post. Reinvent Albany, a government watchdog focused on transparency and accountability, has said it supports city agencies using paid social media influencers to promote government programs but opposes city officials using instant-messaging apps such as Signal for official communications. MAMDANI SPARKS FEARS OF VIOLENCE AFTER DOXING WEALTHY NYC PROPERTY OWNERS: 'OUTRIGHT DANGEROUS' In testimony before the New York City Council earlier this month, the group warned that the city still lacks a practical way for agency Freedom of Information Law officers to archive or retrieve official records created on apps such as Signal. "Even now, in 2026, the City of New York has not developed a practical way for official records created by these apps to be archived or retrieved by agency FOIL officers," Reinvent Albany testified. The watchdog has called for legislation clarifying that electronic and instant messages constituting public records must be preserved and easily retrievable, while also proposing disclosure requirements for influencers paid to promote city messaging. NYC MAYOR MAMDANI CALLS THREAT OF RICH PEOPLE LEAVING NYC OVER TAXES 'IMAGINED' The alleged effort to go after NYC's CEOs comes as Mamdani continues to push for higher taxes on wealthy New Yorkers and corporations to fund his agenda and address the city's budget challenges. Mamdani called earlier this year for a 2% personal income tax increase on New Yorkers earning $1 million or more, alongside an increase in the corporate tax rate. While those proposals did not make it into this year's budget, Mamdani has continued to publicly back both. "I've been very open and honest about my vision, whether it be fast and free buses or whether it be higher personal income taxes on the wealthiest New Yorkers or the most profitable corporations," Mamdani said in May. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The mayor did secure a new pied-à-terre tax on luxury second homes owned by non-city residents, which his administration projects will generate roughly $500 million annually. The measure was dealt a legal setback Tuesday, however, when a Staten Island judge ordered the administration to scrap its initial rollout and restart the process after finding the city failed to follow required procedures before sending tax notices. The ruling did not strike down the tax itself, and Mamdani's administration vowed to continue fighting for the surcharge. Matt Rauschenbach, a Mamdani spokesman, defended the surcharge as a "basic principle of fairness," arguing that owners of luxury second homes should contribute toward the city services they benefit from.

articles.title: Trump says ‘only a Hispanic could survive’ fall from White House ballroom
articles.summary: President Trump said during a Hispanic Heritage Month event Wednesday that only Hispanics could survive a fall from the site of the White House ballroom. The...
articles.body:
President Trump said during a Hispanic Heritage Month event Wednesday that only Hispanics could survive a fall from the site of the White House ballroom.

The president made the remark in the East Room after inviting the event's attendees to step onto the floor of the new ballroom outside.

"There's a tunnel going to what I think will be the greatest ballroom ever built. It's also a tremendous military complex with a drone port on top," Trump said.

"You literally will be the first group ever to enter the premises. So be very careful. Don't fall over the edge, because it's a long way down," he continued.

"And only a Hispanic could survive that fall," the president added, receiving cheers from attendees. "So, I'm not overly worried."

The Hispanic Heritage Month event Wednesday at the White House is the first of the second Trump administration. The White House did not hold an event honoring the month last year, but the president did sign a proclamation celebrating it.

Trump's remarks to attendees Wednesday lasted nearly an hour and also featured Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the highest-ranking Hispanic official in the U.S.

The event comes as polling shows Republicans struggling with the Hispanic voting bloc, which boosted Trump during the 2024 presidential election.
