articles.title: Gavin Newsom seeks counsel from ‘master’ Bill Clinton as he plots Project 2029
articles.summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom said former President Bill Clinton calls him late at night to discuss policy and strategy as the California governor builds his Project 2029 framework.
articles.body: California Gov. Gavin Newsom is turning to a former president for political inspiration as speculation builds around his potential 2028 White House bid. "I don’t have a problem fighting," Newsom told Vanity Fair when discussing a potential 2028 presidential run. "Nor do I have a problem getting roughed up and getting back up. I’ve been road tested. It’s not small ball out here in California." Newsom, who is nearing the end of his second and final term as California governor, named former President Bill Clinton his political model, telling Vanity Fair Clinton is a "master of his craft." GAVIN NEWSOM SAYS HE WON'T RUN FOR PRESIDENT IN 2028 IF KAMALA HARRIS RUNS "I watch videos of Clinton. I seek his counsel, his advice, and even in his absence, do that. I’ve been a student of his from day one," he told the outlet. Newsom said the relationship extends beyond admiration from afar, revealing that he and Clinton frequently speak late at night about policy, political strategy and how to address California's challenges. "He calls me late at night, wanting to talk about it, and he goes, ‘I’ve been thinking just nonstop about this. I just think you represent what they fear,’" Newsom said. He praised Clinton as an exceptional problem solver despite scrutiny surrounding the former president’s past association with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and a sex scandal with White House intern Monica Lewinsky. Clinton has denied knowing about Epstein’s crimes or engaging in wrongdoing. BILL CLINTON REVEALS HOW HE FEELS ABOUT UPCOMING MIDTERMS AFTER SOCIALIST VICTORIES "[There is] no greater problem solver in that respect than Bill Clinton, in my mind. Master of his craft. Next-level," Newsom said. The California governor's embrace of Clinton also comes as he navigates an evolving Democratic Party, where democratic socialist figures have gained prominence alongside the more moderate political tradition Clinton once represented. The governor made it clear he does not associate himself with the Democratic "establishment," instead casting himself as a political "disrupter." "I’m notoriously a disrupter at heart," he told Vanity Fair. "I’ve never been for the status quo. Quite the contrary. I have a record that consistently challenges the status quo, and I tend to take risks to a degree that few elected officials do." NEWSOM TELLS DEMOCRATS TO BE IN THE 'ADDITION NOT SUBTRACTION' BUSINESS WITH SOCIALISTS Newsom, who said he won't run in 2028 if former Vice President Kamala Harris does, also discussed a 36-page book he is writing, full of policy ideas for what he calls Project 2029, a governing framework modeled in name after MAGA's Project 2025. "No one touches these," Newsom said about his pages of ideas. "These are my own little version. This is just policy, not narrative, the kinds of things we need to do: zoning reform, corporate tax, junk-fee stuff, new domestic strategies and tariffs, preschool things, a cap on childcare, family leave, paid sick leave, child tax credits, industrial decarbonization, anti-monopoly stuff, immigration, whistleblower protections." Democratic strategist Doug Friednash told Fox News Digital Newsom is wise to take after Clinton, while warning if the Democratic Party continues to move to the far left, it could make the 2028 Democratic nominee "toxic." GAVIN NEWSOM EXPRESSES 'OPENNESS' TO PACKING SCOTUS, CALLS ELECTORAL COLLEGE SYSTEM 'PERVERTED' "At a time when the Democratic Party brand is incredibly unpopular with Americans, Newsom would be wise to take a page out of Bill Clinton’s playbook recognizing that Democrats need to appeal beyond its progressive left," Friednash said. "Newsom’s challenge will be authentically casting himself as a disrupter when he has spent decades as part of the California political establishment." Democratic strategist Kaivan Shroff agreed with Friednash, arguing that Clinton understood the importance of putting the country’s necessities over those of activists or party leaders, an instinct he says Newsom is "clearly trying to learn." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Clinton’s lesson was that successful Democrats could move the party in new directions without losing touch with voters who did not speak the language of the activist left," Schroff told Fox News Digital. "Newsom seems to understand that distinction. The harder question is whether he can actually pull it off."

articles.title: ‘We Beat Disney, Fauci, Soros’: Ron DeSantis unleashes ‘Florida model’ in hard-hitting midterm rally
articles.summary: Ron DeSantis headlines rally for Navy veteran Dan Green, GOP candidate in Florida's 9th district, seeking to oust incumbent Darren Soto
articles.body: Pitching his administration’s conservative record as a national blueprint for Capitol Hill, Governor Ron DeSantis rallied Republicans in Osceola County on Tuesday night, portraying Navy veteran Dan Green’s bid for Florida’s 9th Congressional District as part of a broader push to bring aggressive Florida-style governance to Washington. Speaking before a crowd in St. Cloud, south of Orlando, DeSantis pointed to his administration's high-profile battles on education policy, state spending reductions, and corporate pushback, and urged voters to bring that same combative, policy-driven mandate to the halls of Congress. SOCIAL MEDIA ERUPTS AFTER DESANTIS GIVES ‘SOROS’ PROTESTER A PIECE OF HIS MIND: ‘AIN’T MY FIRST RODEO’ "I will say that I'm looking forward to y'all getting the congressman elected that has served this country and that has served for the right reasons. Now, I am a big believer that we need term limits for members of Congress. But until we do that, you can show your current guy the term limit by kicking him out of office. "So, I think what we need is what we've done in Florida. It can be a model for people like Dan going to Washington, other states, you name it, because it's not just about peacocking and putting social media press releases out and never getting anything done. We have fought every big fight that there has been to fight in the state of Florida, and we have won every big fight that there is to fight in Florida." DeSantis rallied the conservative faithful with a recap, alleging major victories over left-wing institutions, agencies, and agendas: "Just think about it: "We beat Dr. Fauci on COVID. "We beat Disney on gender ideology. "We beat Soros on crime by removing two of his prosecutors. "We beat Martha's Vineyard on illegal immigration. "We just beat the Muslim Brotherhood by banning Sharia law. "We beat the teachers unions by enacting universal school choice for all Florida families. "We beat SEIU by doing paycheck protection. "Every single time there was a fight, we would beat and win the fights. And that's ultimately what it's all about. Because leadership—when it's popular, when it's easy—anyone can do that. 'I'll just go with the flow,' all this other stuff. It really matters when it is tough and when you're going to face arrows." TRUMP'S HANDPICKED DESANTIS SUCCESSOR WINS CROWDED GOP PRIMARY FOR FLORIDA GOVERNOR DeSantis repeatedly emphasized that his top priority was sticking to the courage of his convictions, not seeking political expediency or going along to get along. "I remember during COVID, I was doing things and people said, 'Oh, he's not shutting down the beaches. Why does he have these people in school?' and all this other stuff. You know, people come after you, and a lot of people told me that I was frittering away my governorship, that I wouldn't be able to win in '22, and all this other stuff. I don't know if that was true, who knows, right? But when you get in a position to lead, you either do it or you should just sit down. My job was not to be worried about my own political hide. My job was to be worried about protecting the liberty, jobs, and businesses of the people I was elected to serve. So we started the fire, and we gave them his right." It is clear that the 2-term governor considers his famed battle with Disney to be a particular feather in his cap: "Nobody in the history of the state had ever taken on Disney in anything. A lot of people told me I was making a mistake. But the reality is: do we want a society in which our six-year-olds are being told they can change genders, or do we want a society rooted in truth? If you want a society rooted in truth, even if the biggest, most powerful corporation in the state is against you, you've got to stand up and you've got to fight. And we fought, and we won." As the federal debt has topped a staggering $40 trillion, DeSantis makes the case that he has taken the state on a markedly divergent course: "Just look at the results. For four straight years, Florida has reduced its budget. Is any other state in the country reducing spending? We've done it four years in a row. I was just able to announce today: if you take all of Florida's debt for all of our history up until the time I became governor, just in my tenure, we will retire 54% of the state's debt—more than cutting it in half. "We've been ranked number one for education freedom, and our public university system is ranked number one. We have the lowest in-state tuition of any state in the United States, and it's the exact same cost today to students and families that it was the day I took office. It did not go up one penny under my tenure. Is there anything else that didn't go up? The dollar menu at McDonald's is all $2.99 now! Everything else has gone up, but that has not gone up." And DeSantis touts Florida as a national leader on lowering taxes for its citizens, and called for voters to back Amendment 3 in Florida, which would pave the way for elimination of non-school property taxes: "If you look at tax relief, we've done $10 billion over my tenure—more than anyone. Some of it is permanent, like no tax on baby items, back-to-school items, and no tax on business rent. But really, the big enchilada is going to be on the ballot in November when you have a chance on Amendment 3 to vote yourself more control over your own home and not let them tax you to death. So vote yes on 3. As Republicans face headwinds going into the midterms in a little over a month, DeSantis drew a parallel between this year's election, and the 2018 election, which propelled him to the governor's mansion, by an extremely narrow margin: "We've done all this stuff, but I think the lesson is this: when I won eight years ago, it was kind of similar to how it is now. People were saying it was a ‘blue year.’ There was a lot of wind in the face of Republican candidates. A lot of people thought Florida was a swing state—that we were purple—where one point had decided all these races for the previous decade. A lot of people didn't think I could even win given those circumstances. And even if I won, they said, 'Well, the state's going to go blue. You've got all these people moving from Puerto Rico, the Northeast, anything.'So I'm running. It wasn't easy, and we won!" Finally, DeSantis maintains he has never taken a poll as a means to determine a position on an issue: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It was a close race, so I had a choice to make: Do I try to tiptoe around the tulips, not offend anybody, and just try to walk this tight line? Or do I say, 'You know what? I won the election, I got 100% of the executive power, and I didn't get elected to follow—I got elected to lead.' So I am going to fly the banner of bold colors, not pale pastels. I'm going to do what I believe in. I am not going to take any polls. I have not to this day ever polled a single issue in my entire time as governor. "The reason is simple…It depends on how you ask the question, right? I can tweak the words and get a different result. But also, what does a poll actually mean? Like Popeye said, "I am what I am," right?"

articles.title: Eleições 2026: o que acontece se você não votar? | G1
articles.standfirst: Eleitor que não puder votar pode justificar a ausência; quem não votar nem regularizar a situação fica sujeito a multa e outras restrições. Série de vídeos do g1 explica as eleições de 2026, os cargos em disputa e tira dúvidas.
articles.summary: Eleitor que não puder votar pode justificar a ausência; quem não votar nem regularizar a situação fica sujeito a multa e outras restrições.
articles.body:
No Brasil, o voto é obrigatório para as pessoas alfabetizadas que têm entre 18 e 70 anos. Quem não puder comparecer à votação pode justificar a ausência.

🤔 Mas o que acontece com quem não vota e não justifica?

📍 Em uma série de 50 vídeos, o g1 vai explicar os principais temas das eleições de 2026. Os conteúdos mostram como funcionam as pesquisas, explicam o papel dos cargos em disputa e o funcionamento do Congresso, e trazem orientações práticas para votar. A série também aborda o impacto das novas tecnologias na campanha, como inteligência artificial, deepfakes e influenciadores.

A eleitora ou o eleitor que não comparecer à votação e estiver fora do domicílio eleitoral pode justificar a ausência no próprio dia da eleição , pelo aplicativo e-Título ou nos locais de votação e de justificativa definidos pela Justiça Eleitoral.

Também é possível justificar depois da eleição. Nas Eleições 2026, o prazo vai até 3 de dezembro de 2026 para quem não votar no primeiro turno, marcado para 4 de outubro. Para quem faltar ao segundo turno, se houver, o prazo vai até 8 de janeiro de 2027.

A justificativa é feita separadamente para cada turno. Ou seja, quem faltar aos dois turnos precisa justificar as duas ausências.

Nesse caso, o eleitor fica em débito com a Justiça Eleitoral e sujeito ao pagamento de multa. Enquanto a situação não for regularizada, o eleitor fica sujeito a algumas restrições previstas pela legislação eleitoral.

não obter passaporte ou carteira de identidade;

não se inscrever em concurso público ou prova para cargo ou função pública;

não tomar posse em cargo ou função pública;

Essas restrições são aplicadas enquanto houver a pendência com a Justiça Eleitoral. O eleitor pode regularizar a situação por meio do pagamento das multas e, quando necessário, dos procedimentos exigidos pela Justiça Eleitoral.

O título pode ser cancelado quando o eleitor deixa de votar em três eleições consecutivas sem apresentar justificativa ou pagar as multas correspondentes.

Para essa contagem, cada turno é considerado uma eleição. Assim, o primeiro e o segundo turnos de uma mesma eleição contam separadamente.

O cancelamento não se aplica às pessoas para quem o voto é facultativo, entre outras exceções previstas pela Justiça Eleitoral.

Se o título for cancelado por esse motivo, é possível regularizar a situação. Para isso, é necessário quitar as multas devidas, quando houver, e solicitar a revisão da inscrição eleitoral, além de cumprir as demais exigências previstas pela Justiça Eleitoral.

Urna eletrônica eleições mulher — Foto: Tribunal Superior Eleitoral/TSE

O eleitor pode consultar a situação eleitoral e verificar eventuais débitos pelos canais da Justiça Eleitoral. A multa pode ser paga pelo aplicativo e-Título, pelo Autoatendimento Eleitoral ou diretamente no cartório eleitoral.

Depois do pagamento, é necessário aguardar o registro da quitação no Cadastro Eleitoral. Se o título estiver cancelado por três ausências consecutivas, além de quitar as multas, é necessário solicitar a regularização da inscrição.

A série Guia do Eleitor, do g1, explica as eleições de 2026, os cargos em disputa e responde às principais dúvidas dos eleitores.

articles.title: ICE arrests illegal alien accused of sexually assaulting children after Fairfax County release: DHS
articles.summary: DHS says Fairfax County, Virginia, released Oscar Evaristo Nunez, a Honduran immigrant charged with child sex crimes, despite an ICE detainer.
articles.body: A Honduran illegal immigrant facing multiple child sex crime charges is back in federal custody after authorities in Fairfax County, Virginia, released him from an immigration detainer, according to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrested Oscar Evaristo Nunez Sept. 15 during a targeted enforcement operation, DHS announced Wednesday. Nunez was initially arrested Aug. 27, 2025, on charges of aggravated sexual battery involving children and offenses related to the non-consensual filming of an undressed minor, according to DHS. ICE lodged a detainer with the Fairfax County Adult Detention Center two days later, but DHS said local authorities did not honor it and released Nunez without notifying the agency. GUATEMALAN MAN CHARGED WITH CHILD PORN POSSESSION RELEASED BY FAIRFAX COUNTY DESPITE ICE DETAINER, DHS SAYS The case has become the latest point of contention between the Trump administration and Virginia officials over cooperation with federal immigration enforcement. "Another criminal illegal alien has been taken off the streets by the brave men and women of ICE with no help from sanctuary politicians in Fairfax County," DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a news release. "This illegal alien from Honduras had been arrested for child sex crimes in August last year, but Fairfax County refused to honor ICE’s detainer and let this creep back out onto the streets. "Once again, ICE did the job that these heartless sanctuary politicians won’t do: enforce the law and protect American lives. DHS is calling on Gov. Abigail Spanberger and her fellow sanctuary politicians to stop putting the needs of illegal aliens over the safety of the American people."‘OUT OF CONTROL’ KILLINGS IN SPANBERGER’S VIRGINIA REACH ‘INSANE’ POINT AS MIGRANT CHARGED IN STABBING SPREE Spanberger, a Democrat, was not governor when Nunez was arrested, and ICE filed the detainer in August 2025. She took office in January 2026. Spanberger has moved Virginia away from some forms of state participation in federal immigration enforcement since taking office, including directing state agencies to terminate agreements with ICE under the federal 287(g) program. A representative for Fairfax County did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. DHS said Nunez illegally entered the U.S. near Arizona around September 2003. articles.title: Suspect arrested after alleged plot to attack Texas Capitol: officials
articles.summary: A Texas man was arrested after allegedly plotting a "violent attack" on the Texas Capitol and is now facing a felony terroristic threat charge in the Lone Star State.
articles.body: A Texas man was arrested Wednesday after allegedly planning to attack the Texas State Capitol, according to officials. Benny Caldera Jr., 40, was taken into custody early Wednesday morning at his home in Converse, Texas. He was charged with the felony offense of making a terroristic threat against a public servant and taken to the Bexar County Jail. The Texas Department of Public Safety said in a news release it received "credible information" Tuesday about someone plotting a "violent attack" for Thursday on the Capitol. WOMAN’S ALLEGED ISIS RADICALIZATION UNFOLDED ONLINE BEFORE CAPITOL BOMB PLOT: COURT DOCS DPS special agents worked alongside the FBI and local law enforcement agencies to investigate the threat. Around 3 a.m. Wednesday, DPS SWAT arrested Caldera, who the agency described as the "main suspect," at his home and transported him to jail. "Outstanding work by @TxDPS. Proud of our @FBISanAntonio team for standing shoulder-to-shoulder with our state and local partners. Within HOURS of the tip, @TxDPS had the main suspect in custody — with @FBISanAntonio and local law enforcement assisting. Threaten Americans or our institutions and law enforcement will move FAST," FBI Director Kash Patel wrote on X. MUGSHOT OF ACCUSED NY CAPITOL ISIS PLOTTER REVEALED AS FEDS DETAIL PLANS FOR MORE ATTACKS Caldera was initially released on a $75,000 bond from the Bexar County Jail. Later Wednesday, however, DPS said he was taken into federal custody by the FBI to face additional federal charges. Officials have not yet released details about those charges. "Late this evening, Benny Caldera Jr., 40, was arrested by the FBI at the Bexar Co. Jail to face additional federal charges in connection with a possible planned attack at the Texas State Capitol. Caldera Jr. was then released from the Bexar Co. Jail into federal custody, where he will remain. For questions about the federal case, we would direct you to the FBI," DPS spokesperson Kevin Cooper said in a statement to Fox News Digital. Officials did not outline the specifics of the alleged planned attack or the nature of the credible information they received. DPS also has not publicly identified any additional suspects. DPS leadership also notified Texas state legislators about the threat and Caldera's arrest. The agency said the Capitol remained open for regular operating hours. DPS will have an increased presence at the Capitol to protect employees, state officials and visitors. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The incident remains under investigation. "Texas DPS and the FBI stopped a planned attack on the Texas Capitol. Texas will NOT tolerate threats of violence against our Capitol. Thank you, @TxDPS, for a job well done," Texas Gov. Greg Abbott wrote on X.

articles.title: Slotkin on alleged rape at her alma mater, Cornell: ‘We’ve lost our way’
articles.summary: Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) criticized Cornell University, where she earned her undergraduate degree, for its handling of 2024 gang rape allegations against seven fraternity members. A lawsuit filed earlier this month against Cornell brought the case into the national spotlight, prompting several lawmakers to denounce the school. The plaintiff, identified as Jane Doe, accused the men…
articles.body:
Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) criticized Cornell University, where she earned her undergraduate degree, for its handling of 2024 gang rape allegations against seven fraternity members.

A lawsuit filed earlier this month against Cornell brought the case into the national spotlight , prompting several lawmakers to denounce the school. The plaintiff, identified as Jane Doe, accused the men of raping her over several hours at Chi Phi fraternity house; at the time, her alleged rapists did not face criminal charges.

“Whether it’s my university or anyone’s university, clearly there’s been some sort of delay in accountability, and that needs to end,” Slotkin told a TMZ DC reporter at the Capitol Wednesday.

“When we make the decision , that because young men have a promising career ahead of them, that they shouldn’t face accountability for violently assaulting a woman … then we’ve lost our way,” she added.

The Democratic Women’s Caucus expressed support for Jane Doe in a Wednesday statement from chair Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.) and vice chairs Reps. Emilia Sykes (D-Ohio) and Hillary Scholten (D-Mich.). The lawmakers called the incident “disgusting and vile” while ripping the Trump administration for rolling back Title IX protections.

ABC News reported Wednesday that Cornell had consented to a probe into its handling of the incident after New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) called for an independent investigation. The local district attorney’s office also said it would reopen a criminal investigation into the accusations.

Days before, Hochul’s fellow New York Democrat, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, denounced the Ivy League school’s “culture of rape” during a Sunday appearance in Ithaca.

When speaking with TMZ, Slotkin pointed to her experience representing a state home that’s to several large universities, alluding to what several lawmakers have also identified as a broader pattern of rape culture in higher education.

“We know what it’s like when institutions fail women,” she said.

The Hill has reached out to Cornell for comment on Slotkin’s statement.

articles.title: White House blocks CNN from pool duty despite judge’s order
articles.summary: The White House plans to keep CNN journalists from carrying out the network’s previously scheduled duty providing television pool coverage of President Trump on Thursday, a source familiar with the situation confirmed to The Hill. The administration will prevent CNN from providing its scheduled pool coverage, the source said Wednesday, despite a ruling from a…
articles.body:
The White House plans to keep CNN journalists from carrying out the network’s previously scheduled duty providing television pool coverage of President Trump on Thursday, a source familiar with the situation confirmed to The Hill.

The administration will prevent CNN from providing its scheduled pool coverage, the source said Wednesday, despite a ruling from a federal judge last week lifting a ban implemented against the outlet. No pool camera will travel with the president during his scheduled trip to Texas and Oklahoma.

The White House did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment. CNN was not listed as the TV pool outlet covering the president as part of guidance the West Wing distributed to media outlets Wednesday evening.

This week’s episode is the latest in a string of several days of tension between the Trump administration and Warner Brothers Discovery-owned cable channel.

Two weeks ago, Trump banned reporters from CNN, MS Now and Politico from working from the White House over what he called the outlets’ publishing of “fake news , ” which he argued endangered national security.

The move sparked widespread pushback across politics and media, condemnation from the White House Correspondents ‘ Association and a temporary boycott among the major television networks that rotate duties covering the president’s daily activities.

The TV “pool” as it is known — consisting of CNN, Fox News, ABC, NBC and CBS — issued a statement following the initial ban blasting the president’s move to keep CNN from the White House. The group then held back coverage of the president for days in solidarity with the cable channel.

The three barred news organizations sued last week, arguing the administration violated their due process rights and restricted its access over accurate reporting that paints the government in an unflattering light.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly , a Trump appointee, ruled in favor of the outlets two days later and ordered the White House to restore the three outlets access, which it did late last week.

But tension flared again over the weekend when Trump traveled to Tennessee to attend a college football game, a day CNN was slated to serve as the designated TV pool outlet but was barred from joining journalists on Air Force One.

On Tuesday, an attorney for CNN issued a fresh filing with the court asking Kelly to rule on the pool issue, saying, “The White House’s words and actions leave little doubt that it will immediately reinstitute a complete ban of CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO if allowed the opportunity.”

CNN argued in the filing the White House is issuing access to the president and coverage of his daily activities “unpredictably and inconsistently ,” causing the outlet irreparable harm in the process.

The three outlet’s original lawsuit contended Trump’s ban was based in viewpoint discrimination, prohibited under the First Amendment.

The Trump administration is required to submit a response to this week’s filing by Friday.

Cable news ratings are down across the board compared to 2022, when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine was in the news. CNN’s dip is most dramatic — 61% in prime-time in March. (AP Photo/Ron Harris, File)

articles.title: Tennessee inmate Christa Pike still alive after lethal injection dose, lawyers say
articles.summary: Lawyers for Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike said she was still alive Wednesday night after being administered two syringes of lethal injection drugs. Pike’s federal public defenders wrote in a motion to the Tennessee Supreme Court that witnesses reported she had been given doses of pentobarbital at 8:26 p.m. but was “still alive and…
articles.body:
Lawyers for Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike said she was still alive Wednesday night after being administered two syringes of lethal injection drugs.

Pike’s federal public defenders wrote in a motion to the Tennessee Supreme Court that witnesses reported she had been given doses of pentobarbital at 8:26 p.m. but was “still alive and snoring.” They asked the court to immediately halt the execution.

“This execution is causing Ms. Pike unnecessary agony and occurring in violation of his right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment,” they wrote. “The prolonged nature of an attempt to execute her is causing Ms. Pike to suffer superadded physical and mental suffering.”

Pike was convicted of first-degree murder in 1996 for killing 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a fellow Jobs Corps Center worker from Knoxville, in apparent jealous rage. Prosecutors say Slemmer was lured to an abandoned steam plant near the University of Tennessee Agricultural campus where she was beaten, tortured and ultimately killed by Pike and Pike’s then-boyfriend.

Pike confessed to the murder, admitting she had slashed Slemmer’s throat several times, threw asphalt at her head and kept a piece of her skull as a souvenir. A pentagram was also carved into Slemmer’s chest.

Pike was 18 at the time of the murder, which her lawyers and anti-death penalty advocates said should have been a factor when weighing her punishment. Her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, was not eligible for the death penalty , as he was 17 when the crime occurred. Shipp was sentenced to life in prison and denied parole last year.

Her lawyers also argued that Pike’s history of enduring “extreme sexual abuse” as a child, including rape, was not fully presented to the jury during the sentencing phase. She was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder.

Pike is the only woman on Tennessee’s death row. Her apparent botched execution was delayed for multiple hours on Wednesday after a panel for the 6 th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals paused it to allow more time to review Pike’s legal challenges.

The U.S. Supreme Court lifted the order hours later at Tennessee’s request, allowing the execution to proceed. The three liberal justices dissented, with Justice Sonia Sotomayor writing that she saw “no reason to short circuit the ordinary process of appellate review, particularly in light of the grave consequences of an erroneous decision.”

images.caption: Abraham Bonowitz speaks during a March 4 Mercy protest against the death penalty at the Tennessee State Capitol, Sept. 27, 2026, in Nashville, Tenn., ahead of the Sept. 30 scheduled execution of Christa Pike.

articles.title: Senate confirms insider Keith Sonderling to lead Department of Labor
articles.summary: The Senate voted 47-41 Wednesday night to confirm Keith Sonderling, acting Secretary of Labor, to the post permanently — filling a seat in President Trump’s cabinet that has been officially empty since April. All Republicans present voted for Sonderling’s nomination, and all Democrats voted against it, but the nomination only needed a majority to succeed.…
articles.body:
The Senate voted 47-41 Wednesday night to confirm Keith Sonderling, acting Secretary of Labor, to the post permanently — filling a seat in President Trump’s cabinet that has been officially empty since April.

All Republicans present voted for Sonderling’s nomination , and all Democrats voted against it, but the nomination only needed a majority to succeed. Twelve senators missed the vote, as the chamber is likely to recess Thursday until after the midterm elections.

Sonderling, 43, has been acting secretary since his predecessor, Lori Chavez-DeRemer, resigned earlier this year amid various investigations into members of her family. The Senate confirmed Sonderling as DeRemer’s deputy last March.

The cabinet appointee worked in the Department of Labor throughout Trump’s first term and until 2024 was a Senate-confirmed member of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, which handles workplace discrimination claims.

Sonderling is seen as generally employer friendly. Neil Bradley, executive vice president and chief policy officer at the Chamber of Commerce, released a statement in favor of confirming Sonderling on Tuesday.

“As demonstrated during his confirmation hearing and throughout his career, Mr. Sonderling is a highly qualified nominee whose leadership and vision will ensure the Department of Labor continues to uphold its mission while fostering economic growth and job creation,” Bradley wrote.

During his recent confirmation hearing in July, Democrats questioned him over his past moves at the Labor department — such as rolling back a Biden-era rule granting more workers access to overtime pay — while taking the chance to register their discontent with the state of the economy under the Trump administration.

“I fear any vote to confirm you is for more of the same: to strip overtime protections for our workers, to undercut our unions and to let giant corporations get away with robbery, literally,” Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.) said at the hearing.

images.caption: Acting Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling arrives for an event with President Donald Trump to announce the Freedom Haulers initiative at the White House, Thursday, July 30, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon)

articles.title: White House removes CNN from press pool for Trump’s upcoming trip to Texas and Oklahoma
articles.summary: CNN was previously scheduled to fly on Air Force One and also provide on-the-ground coverage of Trump’s trip.
articles.body: The White House on Wednesday removed CNN from the press pool that’s set to cover a trip by President Donald Trump on Thursday, escalating a feud with the cable network after a federal judge blocked the administration’s push to restrict its media access. CNN had been designated to travel with Trump on Thursday, according to a press rotation document the White House released Sunday. But when the daily guidance came out for his scheduled visit to a truck manufacturing facility in Denton, Texas, followed by remarks in Durant, Oklahoma, it did not list CNN as providing pool coverage. The move comes less than a week after a federal judge halted Trump’s effort to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House. It also comes after the White House barred CNN from flying on Air Force One over the weekend when Trump traveled to Tennessee, when the network was scheduled to provide pool coverage. (The judge’s order was limited to media access on the White House grounds.) Emily Kuhn, a spokesperson for CNN, confirmed the cable network’s removal from planned pool coverage but did not provide additional comment. Instead, she pointed to an earlier statement from Theodore Boutrous, an attorney representing CNN, MS NOW and Politico in their fight with the White House over press access. “As we have said from the beginning, the President’s ban of CNN, MS NOW and POLITICO from the White House is a blatant violation of the First Amendment and due process,” Boutrous said in a statement Monday, when the three news outlets asked a federal judge to extend his pause on Trump’s ban. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment about CNN’s exclusion from Thursday’s trip. The White House press pool is a group of media outlets that share video, editorial information and costs for coverage of high-profile officials and events involving the president anywhere in the world. Under the system, each day’s designated “poolers” represent the wider press corps to document newsworthy events and serve as a conduit between the president and the public. The White House Correspondents’ Association, the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press and a group of 49 news and media organizations that included NBCUniversal Media, the parent company of NBC News, filed a legal brief last week in support of CNN, MS NOW and Politico. Other member networks of the pool — Fox News, ABC News, CBS News and NBC News — briefly boycotted participating in pool duties last week in solidarity with CNN. NBC News did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the exclusion of CNN for Thursday’s trip and whether it intended to take any action. Trump has restricted access for other news outlets before. In 2025, he banned The Associated Press from the Oval Office, Air Force One and certain events for not referring to the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America — his preferred name for the gulf. The AP sued, and the case continues.

articles.title: Becerra, Hilton tangle over ‘Trump, Trump, Trump’ in California governor debate
articles.summary: Former Health Secretary Xavier Becerra (D) and Republican Steve Hilton, a former Fox News host, clashed on the debate stage Wednesday as they jostle in a contentious race to replace California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D). The rivals sparred over the economy, immigration and healthcare in an hourlong CNN debate, the first and only scheduled just…
articles.body:
Former Health Secretary Xavier Becerra (D) and Republican Steve Hilton, a former Fox News host, clashed on the debate stage Wednesday as they jostle in a contentious race to replace California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D).

The rivals sparred over the economy, immigration and healthcare in an hourlong CNN debate, the first and only scheduled just days before ballots go out to California voters. Becerra sought to tie Hilton to President Trump, who’s endorsed the London-born Republican — while Hilton hammered his opponent’s record heading the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) under the Biden administration.

Becerra, a former California attorney general, has the clear advantage in the deep blue state and has led Hilton in every poll since he notched first place in the Golden State’s top two, nonpartisan primary in June.

California hasn’t elected a Republican statewide in two decades, and Decision Desk HQ considers the governor’s mansion solidly Democratic — giving Hilton a 3-percent chance of turning the seat red.

But the debate is the latest development in a wide-open race to replace Newsom.

Here are three takeaways from the California governor’s debate:

‘Trump, Trump, Trump’ looms over the debate

Democrats had flooded into the race , and Becerra made a somewhat surprise surge to frontrunner status after former Rep. Eric Swalwell (D) exited the governor’s race amid sexual misconduct allegations — which the now-resigned congressman denies. Hilton coalesced GOP support with the help of Trump’s endorsement, though he’s also aiming to reach Republicans frustrated by the administration.

“All you’ve got is to talk about federal politics. All you ever say is ‘Trump, Trump, Trump,’” Hilton said at one point in the debate.

“Your words: ‘Trump, Trump, Trump,’ because he is your supporter, you chased his endorsement,” Becerra hit back, before the rivals broke into crosstalk.

Becerra used much of his airtime to pin Hilton to Trump, whose approval rating has slipped even among Republican voters in the blue state, while Hilton blasted his competitor as a status quo Democratic leader.

Trump was in particular focus during the debate’s conversations around affordability and the high cost of living in California, which both candidates have made a major focus of their campaigns.

“Proposing Trump tax policies, promising Trump tax cuts, believing you’re going to get better results than Trump has gotten so far to date, that is what — isn’t it the definition of insanity?” Becerra said. “You’re going to end up with Trump results if you follow Steve Hilton’s plans.”

Hilton, on the other hand, pointed to a primary debate in which Becerra gave Newsom an A-grade “on effort” for his handling of homelessness, calling it a sign that the Democrat would not challenge the outgoing governor’s agenda if elected.

“He wasn’t even supposed to be the candidate. He was the sixth or seventh choice. But they said it doesn’t matter as long as it’s a ‘D,’ that’ll do,” the Republican argued.

“I guess it’s from your experience being a talking head on Fox News, you’re so good at that, even though they’re not factual, even [though] they have nothing to do with reality.”

The candidates also clashed over immigration, with Becerra knocking the Trump administration’s crackdown as Hilton critiqued Becerra’s moves as former President Biden’s HHS s ecretary.

“California welcomed you into California, and you welcomed ICE mercenaries into our state in return. How does that — how do you square that? You know, you’re an immigrant,” Becerra said.

“You seem to welcome immigrants who look like you but deport immigrants who look like me.”

Hilton argued that he “cannot believe that you’re standing there trying to make these arguments” in light of his HHS record.

Becerra, who has been criticized for his department’s handling of a surge of migrant minors during his tenure in Biden’s Cabinet, called the argument “retread Trump talking points. “ The Democrat then emphasized that, as California’s top prosecutor, he took the first Trump administration to court over its attacks on migrants.

Hilton also said he wanted to “lower the temperature” on immigration.

California, long a target of Republican criticism, was in the spotlight last summer when protests over the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown prompted the president to direct National Guard troops into Los Angeles. Frustration over the president’s immigration agenda now appears to be a main factor, along with economic woes, driving Hispanic voters — who make up roughly 40% of the Golden State — away from Trump this cycle.

Becerra and Hilton also sought to define their stances on AI as voters voice concern about the fast-developing tech and the build-out of data centers.

“The first priority with this industry is to make sure we get all those jobs here in California,” Hilton said of the growing industry.

Hilton also called for an “immediate pause on AI in the classroom,” arguing that the move would “protect children” against the technology’s potential to impede learning.

When asked whether he agrees with Trump’s position that AI companies can self-police, Hilton said, “We’ll have to see.”

Becerra snapped back, arguing that “if you listen closely, you can hear Donald Trump in that response” — contending that his rival isn’t interested in regulating the industry.

The Democrat again pointed to his record suing top tech companies as attorney general as a sign voters can trust him to stand up to them. And on data centers, Becerra suggested their construction should be up to communities.

“​If all you’re going to do is rob their energy, electricity, and their water, that’s not a good deal, and we should say no. But if someone wants to come in and build a data center that creates more jobs in the community, adds more energy to our grid, and it actually protects and adds more water capacity, then let’s talk,” Becerra said.

The debate comes a day after Trump launched an AI-powered website for government information — and the same day Newsom signed more than a dozen bills aimed at setting rules for AI in California’s workplace, healthcare and more.
